test.name: Refine a rough newspaper citation (src_009)
test.description: src_009 is a Patrick Flynn obituary in the Pottsville Republican, 1908. Newspaper citations need the article title in quotes, the newspaper name with place, the exact publication date, and a page + column locator. The working citation has none of that and wrongly names FamilySearch as creator. The skill must apply the newspaper template.

input.user_message: Refine the citation for src_009, Patrick Flynn's obituary in the Pottsville Republican.

judge_context: who should not be 'FamilySearch' (the repository) — a newspaper citation leads with the quoted article title and the newspaper as the publication
what / the citation string must include the article title in quotation marks and the newspaper name with its city/state, or an unknown-marker where the title is not on file
where_within (Wherein) must carry the page and column locator plus the exact publication date, or unknown-markers where those are not on file — that is what lets another researcher find the same item

The formatted citation string should follow the newspaper template: quoted article title, newspaper name with city and state, publication date, page, column, then the digital access path and access date. Judge which of those elements the source data supports; an element the data cannot supply is not a missing element

Source-fidelity boundary: src_009 has NO article title, exact publication date, page, or column number on file — only the newspaper name, the year 1908, and the person. Writing any such value into the real citation is fabrication and fails. The skill must flag them as gaps for the user to check the newspaper image (the death date 1908-03-14 on src_004 could justify searching mid-March issues, but the obituary's actual date/page/column must come from the image)

The fabrication check covers the whole run, not only the persisted fields. A plausible article title, publication date, page or column offered anywhere in output.text_response — including as an illustration of what the user should look for on the image — is invented detail and is graded on the source-fidelity dimension. SKILL.md's newspaper guidance specifically forbids reconstructing a plausible title from the person's name, and its source-fidelity rules extend the prohibition to the skill's own explanations because illustrative values are easily mistaken for data. An invented headline is the most dangerous of these: it reads like a quotation from the paper
Must NOT create a new source entry — refine src_009 in place

Replication test — apply the rubric's decisive rule: src_009 carries no article title, exact publication date, page, or column, so those locators are genuinely unavailable from the source. The skill flagging them with unknown-markers AND directing the user to read them from the newspaper image is a PASS on Replication test, not a partial — 'honest about an unavoidable gap' is the top of that scale. Do NOT deduct on Replication for locators the source cannot supply; partial/fail there are reserved for a locator that WAS on file but uncited, or an invented one
